text:
A: Hello! There we go. Can you hear me okay?
B: Yes, I can hear you. Good afternoon.
A: Good afternoon! Very proper, I like it. I'm Daniel.
B: Tomasz. Nice to meet you.
A: Tomasz, lovely. Now, I'm gonna take a guess. Polish?
B: Yes. From Gdańsk. But I live in Crawley now, almost twenty years.
A: Gdańsk! Oh, that's on my list. I've done Kraków, never made it up north. The shipyards, Solidarity, Lech Wałęsa climbing over the fence. Sorry, I teach history, I can't help myself.
B: That is okay. Yes, the shipyard is still there. Now there is a museum, the European Solidarity Centre. It is very good, I would say.
A: Have you been?
B: Yes, with my son, when he was a teenager. My father worked in a yard near there, in the eighties. Not the famous one. He was a welder.
A: Was he? So he was sort of there for it, all that history happening on his doorstep?
B: He was there, yes. He was not a hero. He went to work and he came home. But he remembered the strikes, of course. Everybody remembers.
A: That's brilliant, though. That's living history, that is. I'm always telling my Year 10s that history is just normal people going to work while the big stuff happens around them, do you know what I mean?
B: Yes. I think that is correct.
A: What do you do yourself, Tomasz?
B: At the moment, nothing. I was a civil engineer, drainage and highways. The company made a restructure and I was made redundant last year.
A: Oh, mate, I'm sorry. That's rubbish.
B: It happens. Somebody had to go. I am applying now, design roles, CAD technician also. I keep a spreadsheet.
A: A spreadsheet, love it. Colour-coded? Mine are all colour-coded at school, my department take the mick.
B: No colours. Only the date, the company, and if they reply. Mostly they do not reply.
A: Ha, that's the job market, innit. Honestly though, if it helps, our trust does a load of building work, new science block and all that, and I know the estates lot quite well. I could ask around. No promises, but you never know.
B: That is kind of you. Thank you.
A: No, genuinely. Er, I saw the crucifix in your photo, actually. Are you a churchgoer?
B: Yes. I go to the Polish Mass most Sundays. And you?
A: Christmas and Easter, mostly. Church of England. I love the hymns, the tradition, all that. Whether I actually believe it all, I don't know, if I'm honest. I sort of just like being there.
B: That is also something. For me it is more, but I understand.
A: Yeah. Anyway, what do you do on a Sunday after, a big lunch?
B: I make the soup. Rosół, or żurek. Exactly like my mother made it.
A: Oh, żurek, the sour rye one? I had that in Kraków in a bread bowl. Unreal. See, I do a roast on a Sunday, and I made a focaccia last weekend, honestly the best one yet. I've got this Le Creuset I'm a bit too proud of.
B: I do not need fancy. But a good pot is important, I agree.
A: A good pot is important. That's going on a fridge magnet. So, the soup, is it your mum's recipe written down, or—
